conversation_lines.text: We’re tracking that too. Your readings have been stable. We’ll keep managing it with your current meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been here a few days now. How are you feeling emotionally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still down, but the voices are quieter. I haven’t had any thoughts about hurting myself since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s really good progress. I’m proud of you for staying safe and engaging in treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to go home, though. Everything that triggers me will still be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely valid. We’ll set you up with outpatient therapy and a psychiatrist. You won’t be alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your J-tube is functioning well. The nursing team says it’s easy to flush now and no kinks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Last time it got blocked, I ended up in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you clear instructions on care so you can manage it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain? It’s still there, even with the methadone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not eliminating the pain, but we want to help you manage it better. The combination of meds and therapy should help reduce how much it controls your life.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day we’re planning to discharge you. How do you feel about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, but also kind of ready. I don’t want to stay in the hospital forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made real progress. You’re no longer having suicidal thoughts, your mood is more stable, and your J-tube is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sertraline, mirtazapine, quetiapine at night, and continued methadone. Allergies are flagged—no milk products or trigger foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And therapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have an appointment next week with Dr. Lin, and we’ve scheduled follow-up with your pain specialist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I don’t say it enough, but… thank you for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re strong for coming in and doing this work. Keep reaching out if you need help. We’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. The instructions are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember, if the voices come back or you feel unsafe, go to the ER or call your crisis line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I want to stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge order is in. You’ll be leaving later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. It feels like a fresh start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: meds packed, follow-ups scheduled, J-tube care instructions reviewed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard this week. Keep going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling anxious as I pack. What if I slip back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s normal to worry. But you have tools now—meds, therapy, support. And you’ve proven you can reach out. That’s huge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Ready to go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: As ready as I’ll ever be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. We’re just a call away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe and keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m going to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had really bad stomach pain for about a week. It started with nausea and vomiting, even a fever. I thought it was just another flare of my pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you have a history of chronic pancreatitis. Did making yourself NPO—no food or drink—help at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It usually helps, but this time it didn’t. The pain just kept getting worse, especially in my upper belly and back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve started you on IV fluids and some medications for pain and nausea. Your labs show mild inflammation, but no signs of severe infection or organ failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just so tired of this. I’ve been admitted so many times for this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that. We’re going to focus on controlling your pain and keeping you hydrated. We’ll keep you NPO for now to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on IV pain meds the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’re using IV Dilaudid, Ativan, Phenergan, and Benadryl. These help with pain, anxiety, and nausea. We’ll transition to oral meds when you’re ready to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had bad reactions to some pain meds before. I’m allergic to morphine, Zofran, Reglan, and Imitrex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for reminding me. I’ve noted those allergies. We won’t use any of those. The meds you’re on now are safe for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your vitals are stable, and your pain seems a bit better. We’re going to keep you on IV fluids and meds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a little better, but still uncomfortable. Can I try some food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to make sure your pancreas is fully rested. We’ll reassess tomorrow. Your lab work is improving—your white count and liver enzymes are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just worried about getting weaker. I have my J-tube—can we use that for nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your J-tube earlier—it’s in good position. But for now, we’re holding off on feeds to let your pancreas heal. We’ll consider it if this goes on much longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is definitely improving. We’re going to start transitioning you to oral tramadol for pain instead of IV Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep the IV Dilaudid available just in case? I get really anxious if I think I won’t have pain relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep it written for now, but we’re moving toward oral meds. Your pain management doctor agreed with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve had issues before when pain meds were stopped suddenly. I don’t want to feel like I have to leave the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not stopping anything abruptly. We’re tapering safely. And we’re monitoring your mental health too, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ve been through a lot, especially with depression and anxiety. I’ve had suicidal thoughts before, but I’m not feeling that way now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. Your psychiatric meds—like sertraline, mirtazapine, and quetiapine—are being continued. We want to keep everything stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to stop the IV Ativan and switch to oral lorazepam as needed. Same with Benadryl—we’ll switch to hydroxyzine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it okay if I still have the IV Phenergan available? I’ve used it for years for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it written until discharge, but we’ll encourage oral promethazine afterward. It works the same way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to make sure I’m not left without options when I go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’re going to reconcile all your medications so you have a clear list. There were some differences in your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I admit I don’t always take them exactly as prescribed. Sometimes I skip my blood pressure pills if I feel dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but lisinopril and Toprol are important for your heart. Your EF improved from 30% to 50%, which is great—we want to keep that progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to be more consistent. I just hate the side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can adjust doses if needed. But don’t stop them suddenly. That can be dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your pain is much better, and you’ve been tolerating small sips. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What meds will I be going home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your list. You’ll continue amitriptyline, mirtazapine, sertraline, and quetiapine for mood and sleep. Buspirone and lorazepam for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take Seroquel and Ambien. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to zolpidem instead of Ambien—it’s the same drug. And quetiapine is replacing Seroquel; it’s the same medication, just a different brand name.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. And what about pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on tramadol 75mg every 6 hours as needed. No other narcotics. This was agreed upon with your pain specialist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t get Dilaudid or anything stronger at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless your pain doctor approves it. We’re trying to avoid dependency. Tramadol is safer and effective for most flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I can try. What else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll also take pantoprazole for stomach protection, gabapentin and tizanidine for nerve and muscle pain, and iron supplements for your anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot about the iron. I’ve been so tired lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is low. Take the ferrous sulfate with vitamin C to help absorption, and the docusate and senna to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my J-tube enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take the pancreatic enzymes—two capsules four times a day, including at bedtime. That’s crucial for digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. Your pain is controlled, and you’re back to normal activities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad this flare is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with all your meds and instructions. Follow up with your pain doctor and psychiatrist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I have another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your pain doctor first. If you need to come in, we’ll consult them before giving any narcotics other than tramadol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Thanks for listening to me this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We want you to feel safe and supported. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of chest and abdominal pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about ten days ago I was in a car accident. My car hit a tree, and the airbag didn’t go off. A few days later, I started having chest pain in the front, and it goes down my left arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you go to the ER already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, five days ago. They did a CT scan of my head, chest, and belly. Everything came back normal, but the pain hasn’t gone away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about your stomach pain? Is that new too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, that’s from my pancreatitis. I’ve had it for years. This feels just like my usual flares—nausea, vomiting, sharp pain in my upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll manage both your chest and abdominal pain carefully. Your EKG showed some changes, but your troponin was normal, so it doesn’t look like a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But the chest pain still worries me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We also got a chest X-ray, and it showed no pneumonia or fluid. Your lungs look clear. The pain might be from muscle strain after the accident.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I did feel sore after the crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your pancreas rest. We’ll give you IV fluids and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I have something for nausea? I feel like I might throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you an anti-nausea medication through your IV. Also, because you’re on a lot of pain meds, we’re being cautious. Your pain specialist gave us clear instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did they say?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They recommend IV Dilaudid only if you can’t keep anything down. Once you can eat, we need to switch you to oral tramadol, up to 100mg three times a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on tramadol before. It helps, but sometimes not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll balance pain control with safety. We also want to involve psychiatry and addiction medicine, just to make sure we’re supporting you fully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ve had issues with pain meds in the past, but I’m trying to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’re here to help. We’ve placed a central line in your neck to make giving meds and fluids easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt that earlier. It’s okay, just a little uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal pain is a little better. Still nauseous, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to keep you NPO for one more day, but we’ll start reducing your IV pain meds slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try sipping water today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try small sips later if you’re still not vomiting. We want to be careful not to flare your pancreatitis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You made it through the night without vomiting. We’d like to start you on clear liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Can I have some broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with broth and jello. If you tolerate that, we can advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain? The IV meds are helping, but I know I need to switch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll start you on oral tramadol today—50mg every 6 hours as needed. We’ll watch how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been keeping down liquids and your pain is manageable with tramadol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a little nausea this morning, but it passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a low dose of an anti-nausea med just in case. Also, psychiatry met with you yesterday—how was that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was helpful. They said they’d help coordinate with my therapist after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. They also recommended continuing your antidepressants and anxiety meds, which we’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a regular diet now and your pain is mostly controlled. We’re thinking about discharge in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. What about my chest pain? It’s better, but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe it’s musculoskeletal from the accident. It should keep improving. But if it gets worse, let us know right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need physical therapy for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. But if it doesn’t resolve, your primary doctor can refer you. For now, rest and gentle movement are best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Pancreatic enzymes are coming down. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue tramadol for pain—up to 100mg three times a day as needed. But we’ll taper it as your pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your usual meds—antidepressants, anxiety meds, and we’ll start you on vitamin D since your level was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day in the hospital. You’ve done really well. We’re discharging you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What follow-up do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your pain specialist in one week and your psychiatrist in two weeks. Also, your primary doctor will check your vitamin D and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure was high when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. Your primary will monitor it. If it stays high, they may start a medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—what if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s mild, try tramadol and rest. If it’s severe or you start vomiting, go to the ER. But try to avoid frequent hospital visits if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I know I need to work on managing this long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re here to support you. You’re going home with instructions and prescriptions. A nurse will go over everything before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid driving after the accident?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your chest pain is mild and you’re not on heavy pain meds, it’s probably okay. But if you’re uncomfortable or distracted, wait a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll play it safe and wait until I feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a smart plan. Listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety—sometimes it flares with pain. Any advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your prescribed anxiety meds as directed. Deep breathing, grounding techniques, and staying in touch with your therapist can help a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’re confident you’ll keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. It’s been a tough few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. But you’re taking the right steps. Keep going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping manage your care while you’re here. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’m in a lot of pain, same as my usual pancreas flare—epigastric, radiating to my back. And now I’ve got this chest pressure that goes down my left arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That chest pain—does it get worse with activity or better with rest?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t matter if I’m moving or lying still. But it does get worse when I’m nauseous or vomiting. And it did get better when I took a nitroglycerin tablet under my tongue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. We did an EKG in the ER, and it didn’t show signs of a heart attack. Your troponin levels were also negative. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? I was really scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t look like a typical cardiac issue. The fact that nitroglycerin helped makes us think it could be related to your esophagus—maybe spasms triggered by nausea or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. My stomach’s been so upset—I can’t keep anything down, not even my J-tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your symptoms sound like a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and restart your pain and nausea protocol from your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been on Dilaudid, Ativan, and Phenergan before—it helps a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already started those. You should start feeling some relief soon. We’ll monitor your labs, but your lipase was normal, which is a bit unusual for a flare, but not unheard of.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, sometimes my enzymes don’t spike even when I’m in bad shape.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re treating based on your symptoms and history. We’ll also check your blood pressure—it was a bit high on arrival.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I’ve had hypertension for years. It usually goes up when I’m in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep an eye on it. For now, just focus on resting. I’ll check back in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain and nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still nauseous, but I haven’t vomited since last night. The chest pain hasn’t come back since I took the nitroglycerin yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your repeat troponins were still negative, and your EKG hasn’t changed. We’re confident it wasn’t a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. But why did it feel so similar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the nerves in your chest and abdomen overlap. Pain from your gut can feel like heart pain. And since nitroglycerin relaxes smooth muscle, it might have helped with esophageal spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re going to keep you NPO for now and continue IV fluids. We’ll also monitor your electrolytes—they were a bit low yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. When do you think I can start feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait until your nausea improves more. Maybe by tomorrow, we can try a slow restart through your J-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I just want to feel stable again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. I’ll be back later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. We’re going to place a PICC line today for better IV access. You mentioned antibiotics might be needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of my history of line infections and dental issues. My last bacteremia was from a tooth problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The PICC will let us give antibiotics safely if needed and avoid repeated IV sticks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had PICCs before. The right arm is better for me—I’ve had clots on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. The radiology team will use your right brachial vein. The procedure is quick, under ultrasound guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was placed successfully. It’s in the right brachial vein, tip in the SVC. You did great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I didn’t feel much. Is it ready to use?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s flushed and ready. We’ll continue your meds through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are improving. Hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable. We’re not concerned about bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia for a while. Iron helps, but I don’t absorb it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. More importantly, your nausea is better. Can we try restarting your J-tube feeds at a low rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’d like to try. Start slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start at 20 mL/hour and increase as tolerated. If you tolerate it today, we might advance it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain meds—are we still using Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re spacing it out more. You’re needing less, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I’m turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You are. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your abdominal pain is much improved. You’ve been tolerating the J-tube feeds well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel way better. No nausea, no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep the PICC for now, in case you need antibiotics later. But we’ll remove it before discharge if not needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my blood pressure? It’s still high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s elevated, but likely due to pain and stress. We’ll monitor it. Your primary team can adjust meds if needed after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if all goes well. We’ll discharge you on your regular pain meds, continue J-tube feeds, and follow up with your pain and primary care doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my psychiatrist? I’ve been struggling with depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve noted that. Your psychiatrist will continue managing that. Please keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your abdomen is soft, pain is minimal, and you’re tolerating feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the chest pain returns, especially with exertion, or if you can’t keep feeds down, or pain worsens, come back. Otherwise, follow up in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove it before you leave. You won’t need it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were brought in after a seizure. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… my partner found me on the floor between the bed and nightstand. I don’t remember it. Then 30 minutes later, I had another one—full convulsions. I was confused after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you had a similar episode about three weeks ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I was twitching, foaming at the mouth. Woke up in the ambulance. No loss of bladder or biting my tongue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your records. At that time, your EEG showed some slowing in the left temporal lobe, which can be linked to seizures. But no anti-seizure meds were started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. They said it might be from the pain meds or my pancreatitis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And now, with two more episodes, we’re treating this as likely temporal lobe seizures. Your head CT was normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been having smells that aren’t there—like burning rubber. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a common aura for temporal lobe seizures. It’s a warning sign before the seizure starts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know that. I thought it was just in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s real, and it helps us make the diagnosis. We’ve consulted neurology, and they agree. We’re going to start you on Keppra, an anti-seizure medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help. You haven’t had any since arriving, which is a good sign. We’ll keep you on it and follow up with neurology after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been in a lot of pain from my pancreatitis. It flared up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see. Your lipase is normal, but that can happen with chronic pancreatitis. We’re keeping you NPO for now—no food by mouth—except meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I not even have water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just small sips for now. We’re giving IV fluids and will restart your J-tube feeds soon. We’re also giving Dilaudid for pain through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. The pain is better than last time, but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it controlled. We also gave you ketorolac for inflammation and promethazine for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been dry heaving a bit. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with pancreatitis flares, nausea is common. The promethazine should help. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back—everything looks stable. Your kidney and liver function are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any news on the seizure tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for an MRI today to look for any brain changes. The EEG from before showed left temporal slowing, but no active seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the MRI tell us why this is happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps rule out things like tumors or strokes. Most likely, it’ll be normal, and we’ll attribute the seizures to your medication use and pancreatitis stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking tramadol and lorazepam for pain and anxiety… could that trigger seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially tramadol in high doses. Your tox screen showed methadone too, which wasn’t prescribed. That increases seizure risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know methadone was in my system. I only take what my doctors prescribe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think you may have been getting prescriptions from multiple pharmacies. It’s common with chronic pain. We need to get this under control to prevent more seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want the pain to stop. I don’t want to hurt myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re setting up a plan. We’ll meet with your partner, your PCP, and social work to create a safer medication plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI came back. No tumors, strokes, or signs of acute injury. There are some small white matter changes, likely from aging or blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And no signs of mesial temporal sclerosis, which is good. Your EEG also didn’t show active seizures, just that old slowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s really the meds and stress causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Sleep deprivation, pain, and polypharmacy—especially tramadol and benzos—are likely triggers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been seizure-free since admission, which is excellent. Your pain is improving, and you’ve tolerated small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had toast and applesauce. No nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: And my meds? Can I take my lamotrigine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my anxiety? It’s been worse being stuck here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re on quetiapine and amitriptyline, which help with mood. Let the nurse know if you feel overwhelmed—we can adjust support as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well—tolerating liquids, no vomiting. We’re switching your IV fluids down to 50 cc/hr. Thinking about discharge tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. But what if the pain comes back at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with the same pain meds—tramadol, acetaminophen, ibuprofen when needed. Avoid alcohol and fatty foods. And keep taking Creon with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes to my meds at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Your blood pressure is well-controlled on lisinopril and clonidine. Your heart function is stable too—no signs of cardiomyopathy flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s labs show your white count is down to 7.6—perfect. You’ve had solid food without nausea. We’re planning discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Do I need to follow up with anyone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please see your primary care provider in a week. They’ll coordinate with your specialists—especially for your depression and pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a hard time with depression, especially after my suicide attempt. I know I need help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you’re talking about it. Your care team can help connect you with behavioral health. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my family history—my biological parents both carry a CFTR mutation. Should I be tested?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s worth discussing with your PCP. It may be relevant to your pancreatitis. They can refer you for genetic counseling if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll bring it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re walking, eating, and pain is manageable. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—what if I throw up again or the pain gets bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If you can’t keep fluids down or pain spikes, come back to the ER. But I think you’ll do well with the plan we’ve set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more urine issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been urinating well the last two days. As long as you stay hydrated, it should stay that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to reach out if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had this pain in my upper belly again, like before. It goes into my back. I’ve been nauseous and throwing up bile. I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. How long has this been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About three days. I tried my usual meds—tramadol, Creon, the butalbital for headaches—but nothing’s helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers, chills, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We did a quick X-ray of your abdomen earlier. It shows a lot of stool in your colon—so constipation—but no blockage or free air, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. I’ve been so nauseous I haven’t wanted to eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m allergic to some meds though—Zofran, Reglan, Imitrex, and morphine. I hope that’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that in your chart. We’ll use promethazine for nausea and dilaudid for pain—both are safe for you. We’ll also give Ativan if you’re feeling anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been really anxious. I’ve had depression and panic attacks before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re comfortable. Your labs came back—your liver enzymes and bilirubin are normal, but your alkaline phosphatase is a bit high at 196. Triglycerides are elevated at 460, which can sometimes trigger pancreatitis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that. I’ve had high triglycerides before. Is that why this happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll make sure you have your anxiety meds—lorazepam—as needed. And you can talk to your psychiatrist when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been eating regular food and keeping it down. Pain is much better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had scrambled eggs this morning. Only mild pain now, mostly when I move wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to remove the midline today since you don’t need IV meds anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is there anything I should do differently when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your Creon with meals, stay hydrated, and avoid heavy or fatty foods. Watch your triglycerides—your levels were high but improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I know stress makes it worse too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll keep your anxiety and depression meds consistent. No changes to your usual regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’re walking, eating, and in good spirits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Will I need follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—see your primary doctor in a week for pain management. And your psychiatrist for your mental health meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my constipation? Should I do something about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’re adding docusate and senna to help with that. They’ll make it easier to pass stool without straining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready. Feels good to be better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Just keep up with your meds, eat small meals, and call your doctor if the pain comes back or gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see my PCP and psychiatrist like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your wife is here to pick you up, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s in the waiting room. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are just to be safe?

conversation_lines.text: Mostly from diarrhea and not eating. As you improve, it should stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious, so I’m glad to be back on those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today are excellent. Kidney function is normal, electrolytes are balanced, and liver tests are back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.text: We want to make sure you can handle your home pain meds for at least 24 hours. You’ve been on them since yesterday, so you’re on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. You’ve tolerated your home medications, your infection is treated, and you’re strong enough to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What do I need to do after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the Flagyl and vancomycin exactly as prescribed. Finish the full course, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Six more days. Your last dose will be on October 10th.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your regular meds are restarted—Creon, omeprazole, tramadol, lisinopril, and the others. Take them as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my wife knows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’ve made great progress. Keep taking your antibiotics, stay hydrated, and follow up with your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel lucky to be here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Take care of yourself, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had this terrible stomach pain since last night—right in the middle, near my belly, and it goes into my back. I’ve been vomiting and can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds like your usual pancreatitis flares. Any diarrhea this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to treat this like a flare, but we also need to check for infections. Your labs showed a positive tricyclic screen—was that from your amitriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take that at night. My doctor said it helps with nerve pain and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll hold it for now since you’re not eating. We’re starting IV fluids and your usual pain meds—Dilaudid, Phenergan for nausea, and Ativan if you’re anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That combo usually helps. I’m just so tired of being here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll do our best to get you feeling better quickly. Your blood pressure is a bit high—149 over 76. We’ll watch that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but the pain is a little better. I tried sipping water, but I threw it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re keeping you on IV fluids. We also got your stool test back—it’s positive for C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I had that before, right? That was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in October. We’re starting IV Flagyl and adding oral vancomycin once you can swallow. We need to treat this carefully to avoid complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another PICC line? Last time they put one in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to place one tomorrow for reliable access, especially since you may need longer IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line in your right arm today. It’ll help with antibiotics and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I had a blood clot in my left arm before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re using the right side and ultrasound guidance to make it safe. We’ll also check a chest X-ray after to confirm placement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was placed successfully this morning. The X-ray shows it’s in the right spot—lower SVC. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I feel a little better. I haven’t vomited since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’re continuing IV Flagyl and now adding oral vancomycin for the C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember this from last time. It takes a while, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, usually 10 days or more. We’ll send you home with vancomycin to finish the course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I think I could try some food—maybe broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great sign. We’ll start you on a clear liquid diet and see how you do. Once you tolerate that, we’ll switch back to your oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I restart my amitriptyline? I’ve been having trouble sleeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can restart it with your evening dose. We’ll also continue your lamotrigine and quetiapine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count is down, and your electrolytes are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My stomach still feels bloated, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdomen is still a bit distended, but it’s soft and not tender. That’s a good sign—no obstruction or severe inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It’s been high lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your lisinopril and added a low-dose water pill—HCTZ—to help control it. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re eating soft foods and your pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. You’ll need to finish the vancomycin for C. diff—about 10 more days. And follow up with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I just want to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have all your meds, including Creon for digestion, and your pain and nausea meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check today. Your labs are stable, and you’ve been walking and eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Still tired, but not in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’ve been through a lot. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need isolation at home for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but good hand hygiene is important. Wash thoroughly after using the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my migraines? I’ve had a dull one today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can restart your Fioricet as needed. Just don’t overuse it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll take vancomycin every six hours for the next ten days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll set reminders. And I have my follow-up with my PCP next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. If you develop severe diarrhea, fever, or worsening pain, call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my limits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well this admission. Keep up with your diet, meds, and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can leave once the nurse reviews everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you go. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. I have all my meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Take care, and we hope not to see you back too soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so too. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in to remove your IV and give you final discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your vitamin D and iron levels are still low. Keep taking your supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have them at home. I’ll restart them today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember, stress can trigger flares. Try to pace yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check-in. How are you feeling now that you’re packed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit anxious, but okay. Ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Call your PCP if anything changes. We’re here if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you hopefully never, but thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final reminder—finish all your vancomycin, even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. No shortcuts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’ve come a long way this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I can manage now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your Creon dose is important with meals. Don’t forget it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I know how that goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're here for severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this pain before. It started yesterday—mid-epigastric, really sharp. Nausea and vomiting too. Feels just like my pancreatitis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. You’ve had chronic pancreatitis for a while. Any fever, diarrhea, or blood in your stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or diarrhea. Stools are formed, which is good—last time I was here, I had terrible diarrhea from C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So that’s why I feel so lightheaded?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Fluids should help. We’re also watching your labs—lipase was only 36, which isn’t high, but given your history, we still think this is a pancreatitis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s surprising. I thought lipase always went up during a flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not always, especially with chronic pancreatitis. Your symptoms and history are more telling. We’ll keep you NPO for now and slowly advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Can I try ice chips soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can start those now. We’ll see how you do and try clear liquids tomorrow if nausea improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take Fioricet when I have a bad headache. Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s for my nerve pain and sleep. I take 75 mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re continuing that. Now, your blood pressure is still high—151/99 this morning. Since we held HCTZ, we’re starting lisinopril to help control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I keep taking both when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart HCTZ and add lisinopril. We’ll monitor how you do. Any side effects like dizziness, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been off IV pain meds since last night and are tolerating clear liquids. We’re advancing you to a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! I’m really hungry. Can I have some broth or applesauce?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Start slow. We’ll also switch your pain meds to oral tramadol and keep promethazine for nausea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d prefer that. I don’t want to stay on IV narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great with that. We’re proud of how you’ve stuck to your plan. No extra requests—very responsible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdomen is less tender today, and bowel sounds are normal. You’ve gained a little weight—77.8 kg—so fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. The pain is mild now, just with eating a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’ll keep you on Creon with meals to help digestion. Your omeprazole is also helping with reflux, which can mimic pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to ask—should I keep taking Creon even when I feel fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. It replaces enzymes your pancreas can’t make. Skipping it can trigger flares. Same with amitriptyline and quetiapine—keep those for mood and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve been stable mentally—no dark thoughts or anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll keep your lorazepam for anxiety and insomnia as needed. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re walking, eating well, and off IV meds. How are you feeling about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really good. I’m ready to go home. Will I need the midline removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll remove it before you leave. You won’t need it anymore. We’re sending you home on all your usual meds, including tramadol for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No new narcotics? I’m okay with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re not prescribing any controlled substances. You’ve done so well without extra doses—we trust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I don’t want to depend on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll also give you instructions to follow up with your PCP and continue monitoring your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scan or blood work soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PCP may check labs, but no urgent imaging. Focus on diet—low fat, small meals—and avoid alcohol completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t drink, so that’s fine. And I’ll stick to my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing discharge. Your vitals are stable—BP 151/99, pain minimal. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! My wife is on her way. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Remember: take your meds, follow up, and call if pain worsens or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we hope not to see you back soon!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your contact, your wife, is listed. Call us or her if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’ve done really well this admission. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you in follow-up!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.text: Oh, great! Did it work okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
